additions.sentence: With COPD there can also be periods when symptoms suddenly get worse, known as a flare-up.
additions.evidence: NHS overview: periods when symptoms suddenly get worse, known as a flare-up or exacerbation.

additions.sentence: Pulmonary rehabilitation is a programme of exercise and education that can improve how far someone can exercise before becoming breathless.
additions.evidence: NHS treatment page: a specialised programme of exercise and education that can improve exercise capacity, symptoms, confidence and wellbeing.

additions.sentence: COPD can also come from long-term exposure to harmful fumes or dust, and rarely from a genetic problem that makes the lungs more vulnerable.
additions.evidence: NHS 111 Wales: some cases from long-term exposure to harmful fumes or dust, others a rare genetic problem.

additions.sentence: Having eczema or hay fever, being born prematurely, or growing up around air pollution or cigarette smoke are linked with asthma.
additions.evidence: NHS asthma: risk factors include allergies such as eczema or hay fever, family history, premature birth, childhood exposure to pollution or smoke.

additions.sentence: Asthma can have normal breathing test results at the time of the test, so one normal result does not always rule it out.
additions.evidence: NICE NG245 draft evidence review: asthma is a disease of variable airflow obstruction, so many people with asthma will have normal spirometry at the time.

additions.sentence: NICE says COPD is suspected from symptoms and signs and supported by spirometry, which is also used again if the diagnosis is reconsidered.
additions.evidence: NG115: diagnosis suspected on symptoms and signs, supported by spirometry; repeated when the diagnosis is reconsidered.

additions.sentence: Flu jabs are given at a GP surgery or a taking-part pharmacy.
additions.evidence: NHS living with COPD: vaccinations can be obtained at a GP surgery or participating pharmacy.

additions.sentence: During an asthma attack, sitting up and staying calm is part of the usual NHS advice while using the reliever inhaler as directed, and 999 should be called if there is no improvement.
additions.evidence: Search summary of NHS asthma attack advice: sit up, stay calm, use blue reliever, call 999 if not better or feeling worse.
